resolvedSectionBreaks.before: When the anode voltage varies at a frequency much lower than the oscillator's high-frequency oscillation frequency, the amplitude change can be approximately proportional to the change in anode-to-cathode voltage within the approximately linear operating range of this circuit. This proportionality is a conditional approximation, not an exact relationship guaranteed solely by a large difference between the two frequencies.
resolvedSectionBreaks.after: In this vacuum-tube circuit example, **amplitude modulation** is produced by connecting an additional low-frequency alternating-voltage source in series with the direct-current anode supply. If an audio-frequency current flows through the primary winding of a transformer, its secondary winding can provide this additional source (Figure 114). Under the operating conditions described above, the amplitude of the high-frequency oscillations in the circuit varies with the anode voltage, so the high-frequency oscillations are amplitude-modulated by the low-frequency signal.

resolvedSectionBreaks.after: In some situations, frequency modulation is used as an alternative to amplitude modulation: the frequency of the high-frequency oscillations is varied according to changes in the control signal. This does not mean making the high-frequency oscillation frequency equal to the control-signal frequency. Compared with amplitude modulation, frequency modulation can provide better resistance to interference under suitable transmission and reception conditions, but this advantage is not unconditional for every type of interference.
